edition.deck: Elections, conflict and policy shifts shape the day’s agenda, alongside stories on household costs, public services and life in Denmark.
edition.editorialNote: The selection prioritises consequential developments and strong reporting across the three sections. Distinct accounts of shared events are combined where they add evidence or context; opinion and unresolved allegations remain clearly attributed.

content.headline: Brazil votes in a close Lula–Bolsonaro contest shadowed by corruption claims
content.shortHeadline: Brazil votes in a close contest overshadowed by corruption claims
content.standfirst: Polls put incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro near 40% each. A run-off is likely, with a financial scandal and sharp arguments over crime, the economy and democracy shaping the campaign.

image.caption: The two leading presidential candidates are Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro.

sources.originalTitle: What to know about Brazil's election pitting Lula against Flávio Bolsonaro
The knife-edge election Trump is watching as a blueprint for the midterms

segments.body: Brazilians vote on Sunday in a presidential election led by incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. Polling puts both near 40%, with Lula slightly ahead; if neither wins more than half of valid votes, the two will face a run-off on 25 October. About 160 million people are eligible to vote.

perspectives.body: The i Paper’s commentary frames the election as part of Donald Trump’s effort to influence politics across the Americas. That is the columnist’s interpretation; the report also says the result is expected to go to a run-off.

segments.title: A campaign shaped by corruption and competing priorities
segments.body: A scandal surrounding jailed banker Daniel Vorcaro has put corruption at the centre of the campaign. Police are investigating Flávio Bolsonaro over alleged corruption and money laundering connected to financing a film about his father. Separate allegations have linked Vorcaro to Lula ally and Supreme Court justice Alexandre de Moraes, who denies wrongdoing. Both controversies have become campaign weapons.

Lula points to falling Amazon deforestation as evidence of his environmental record, although his support for exploring offshore oil near the Amazon’s mouth has drawn criticism. Bolsonaro has promised looser regulation and tougher crime policies. The BBC’s polling tracker says 9% of voters were undecided or planned to cast a blank or spoiled ballot, leaving the result uncertain.

content.headline: Russian strikes hit Kyiv’s second major bridge as attacks disrupt city links
content.shortHeadline: Russian strikes hit a second major Kyiv bridge
content.standfirst: An attack on the Northern Bridge injured two people and damaged road and trolleybus infrastructure, after repeated strikes on another crossing. The attacks threaten transport links across the Dnipro and add to pressure on the capital.

image.caption: Technicians repair trolleybus power lines on Kyiv’s Northern Bridge.

sources.originalTitle: Russia hits second major bridge in Ukraine's capital Kyiv
Ukraine war briefing: Kyiv to increase oil refinery attacks because of Moscow’s winter strategy, Zelenskyy says

segments.body: A Russian strike damaged Kyiv’s Pivnichnyi, or Northern, Bridge on Saturday, injuring two people and damaging the road surface and overhead trolleybus wires, Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said. It follows repeated attacks on the Pivdennyi, or Southern, Bridge. Russia says the bridges are used to transfer Ukrainian troops and military cargo.

perspectives.body: In an interview with Reuters, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine would intensify attacks on Russian oil refineries in response to Moscow’s attacks on energy infrastructure, while saying Ukraine would not target civilian sites.

segments.title: A risk to the capital’s connections
segments.body: The bridges link Kyiv’s western and eastern banks across the Dnipro River. Strikes have disrupted road, rail and trolleybus links, while drone threats have restricted other routes and caused traffic congestion. Experts cited by the BBC say repeated attacks could force closures and weaken the bridges, even if drones are unlikely to destroy them outright.

content.headline: Tens of thousands protest across Spain over rents and housing shortages
content.shortHeadline: Thousands protest Spain’s housing crisis
content.standfirst: Demonstrations spread across about 50 cities after parliament rejected emergency measures on rents and evictions. The protests reflect a severe housing shortage and rising costs, while the government’s defeat adds pressure to its fragile parliamentary position.

image.caption: A protest in Spain calls for action on housing costs and tenant protections.

sources.originalTitle: 'Anger in the streets': Tens of thousands protest in Spain over housing crisis

segments.body: Tens of thousands of people marched in Spain on Saturday demanding lower rents, stronger tenant protections and an end to evictions. About 50 demonstrations took place, including in Madrid, Barcelona and Valencia. In Madrid, estimates differed sharply: the Tenants’ Union put attendance at 500,000, while city officials estimated 70,000.

segments.title: Measures rejected as housing pressures mount
segments.body: Parliament rejected two government decrees that included suspending evictions for vulnerable tenants, extending some rental leases, taxing tourist apartments and restricting purchases by investment funds. The government lacks a parliamentary majority, and Together for Catalonia’s opposition helped ensure the proposals failed. The Bank of Spain estimates the country has a housing shortfall of 700,000 homes; house prices rose 12.2% in the year to the second quarter of 2026.

content.headline: UAE says Flydubai co-pilot used cockpit crash axe in alleged attack
content.shortHeadline: UAE says Flydubai co-pilot attacked captain with axe
content.standfirst: The Israel-bound flight plunged sharply before passengers entered the cockpit and helped subdue the co-pilot; reserve pilots landed safely in Saudi Arabia. Investigators are still examining the suspect’s motives and background.

image.caption: Captain Smit Machchhar was praised for his actions during the flight emergency.

sources.originalTitle: Flydubai co-pilot attacked captain with axe, UAE official says
Flydubai co-pilot’s time in Australia being investigated by security agencies after alleged cockpit attack
Flydubai co-pilot used crash axe to attack captain, says UAE
Six things to know as Flydubai pilot used ‘axe in attempted terrorist attack’

segments.body: The UAE prosecutor general says the co-pilot of Flydubai flight FZ1073 used a crash axe to attack the captain and attempt to take control of the aircraft. The plane, carrying more than 170 people, plunged about 17,000 feet before passengers overpowered the co-pilot and two reserve pilots landed it safely in Saudi Arabia.

segments.title: Identity and motive remain under investigation
segments.body: The Indian captain, Smit Machchhar, said he was injured but managed to open the cockpit door so passengers could enter. Several media outlets have named the co-pilot as Hamam, or Hammam, al-Hammami, an Omani national; authorities have not officially confirmed the name. The UAE says investigations into the circumstances, motive and possible connections are continuing.

perspectives.body: The Guardian reports that an official said the co-pilot had been barred from flying in Oman over concerns about extremist views, but it remains unclear how extensively Flydubai vetted him. That claim has not been established as a finding by investigators.

content.headline: G7 agrees to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel amid supply fears
content.shortHeadline: G7 agrees fuel reserve release as diesel supply concerns grow
content.standfirst: The four-month release includes a substantial diesel contribution in its first 20 days. The agreement also rules out energy export restrictions among G7 members, after Donald Trump threatened a US diesel ban.

image.caption: Diesel prices at a petrol station in Bristol have reached a record high.

sources.originalTitle: G7 to release millions of barrels of oil and diesel after Trump threat
Petulant Trump will feel empowered by world’s latest surrender to his demands
Truckers plea for fuel duty bailout as diesel prices hit record high

segments.body: G7 leaders agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel through the International Energy Agency, beginning immediately and continuing over four months. Their statement promises a substantial diesel release within 20 days and says members will not restrict energy exports to one another. It is not yet clear which partner countries will contribute stocks or how quickly.

perspectives.body: The i Paper’s opinion column argues that the agreement shows Trump successfully pressuring allies to release their reserves. It also notes that reserves can be used only once unless replenished.

segments.title: Relief for importers, but not a lasting fix
segments.body: The agreement followed Trump’s threat to ban US diesel exports unless European countries released more of their own stocks. He later said an export ban was never really on the table. The UK imports more than half its diesel, including 31% from the US, and pump prices have topped £2 a litre. Industry representatives warn high fuel costs will feed through to haulage and food prices.

Energy analyst Matt Smith told the BBC that oil prices rose again amid reports of possible Saudi action in Yemen. A University of Salford expert quoted by The i Paper said drawing down emergency reserves offers short-term protection but leaves less cover for future disruption; it does not resolve constraints in refining capacity or reliance on international supply.

content.headline: Cornell president promises review after student’s rape allegations
content.shortHeadline: Cornell president pledges action after rape allegations
content.standfirst: The university president called allegations by a former student deeply disturbing and promised reviews of the case handling. The student’s civil lawsuit alleges she was drugged and assaulted by fraternity members; no charges were laid after the university police investigation.

image.caption: Cornell University is reviewing its handling of a student’s allegations involving a fraternity house.

sources.originalTitle: Cornell president says university 'must do better' after frat house rape allegations
Rektor bryder tavsheden i "dybt foruroligende" sag om gruppevoldtægt
Amerikanske Lindsey elskede studielivet i en studenterforening – men der var også en mørk side

segments.body: Cornell president Michael Kotlikoff said the university “must do better” after a former student, identified in court papers as Jane Doe, alleged she was drugged and raped by seven men from the Chi Phi fraternity in October 2024. She says she reported the incident to university police, who investigated; no charges were laid. Cornell says it is reviewing how the case was handled.

perspectives.body: DR’s interview with former sorority member Lindsey Jensen adds a broader view of campus Greek life: she says sexual assault is normalised in some settings and that a culture of silence can make it harder to challenge. Her account is not evidence about the specific allegations at Cornell.

segments.title: Independent investigations and campus criticism
segments.body: The student filed a civil lawsuit against Cornell last month, alleging the university failed to protect her or adequately discipline those involved. New York Governor Kathy Hochul appointed Attorney General Letitia James to lead a criminal investigation and an independent law firm to review Cornell’s handling. Students have criticised the university at public meetings, while Kotlikoff cited legal and privacy limits on what it can disclose.

content.headline: Russian attacks destroy millions of Ukrainian books and threaten publishers
content.shortHeadline: Russian attacks destroy millions of Ukrainian books
content.standfirst: Strikes on warehouses have destroyed millions of books, including school materials and independent publishers’ stock. Ukrainian officials and publishers say the losses threaten a publishing revival that has become closely tied to language and national identity.

image.caption: Ranok publisher Viktor Kruglov inspects the remains of his burnt-out warehouse.

sources.originalTitle: Incinerated novels and destroyed warehouses: Russia’s war on Ukrainian books

segments.body: A Russian strike on a Kharkiv warehouse destroyed eight million books held by publisher Ranok, including most of its stock, chief executive Viktor Kruglov said. The attack came as the publisher prepared to distribute schoolbooks. The Guardian reports that 50 people were working at the site; no one was injured. Ukraine’s government estimates that 13 million books were destroyed by missiles or drones this summer.

segments.title: A cultural and commercial blow
segments.body: Kruglov believes his book warehouse was deliberately targeted. Deputy culture minister Bohdana Laiuk takes a broader view, saying the strikes are part of attacks on warehouses and fulfilment centres that disrupt everyday life. She also describes the destruction of Ukrainian-language books in occupied areas as part of a longer campaign against Ukrainian cultural identity.

Publishers are trying to reprint textbooks and popular titles, but smaller presses are particularly exposed: independent publisher Krapky lost all its stock in a warehouse strike, and another small press has paused operations. Publishers hope reader support and grants will help them continue, while Laiuk is urging international publishers to translate Ukrainian works.

content.headline: Latvia’s governing party leads election count, rejecting a coalition with Trump-
content.shortHeadline: Latvia’s governing party leads election count
content.standfirst: With most votes counted, Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs’s centrist United List was well ahead of Latvia First, a party inspired by Donald Trump’s movement. Kulbergs has ruled out joining it in government.

image.caption: Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs’s United List led the election count.

sources.originalTitle: Letlands regeringsparti vinder valget
Ukraine war briefing: Kyiv to increase oil refinery attacks because of Moscow’s winter strategy, Zelenskyy says

segments.body: With 88% of ballots counted, Latvia’s governing United List party was on 36.6%, against 13.4% for Latvia First, according to DR. Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs rejected a coalition with Latvia First, which the report describes as inspired by Donald Trump’s movement.

The Guardian’s earlier election briefing, based on 72% of ballots counted, also showed United List well ahead and said populist parties had made gains during a campaign focused on Russia and the cost of living. Kulbergs said his party would not cooperate with parties it considers pro-Russian.

content.headline: Ministers abandon plan to curb jury trials as court backlog nears 100,000
content.shortHeadline: Ministers drop plan to cut jury trials
content.standfirst: The government has changed course after lawyers and MPs opposed expanding judge-only trials. It says a new approach can be introduced sooner, but critics warn the remaining reforms may not be enough to tackle the record crown court backlog.

image.caption: Justice Secretary Alex Norris said ministers had changed course on jury trials.

sources.originalTitle: Ministers drop plans to cut jury trials in England and Wales after outcry

segments.body: Ministers have scrapped plans to replace many jury trials in England and Wales with trials heard by a judge alone. Justice Secretary Alex Norris said he had listened to opposition and wanted to start reducing delays sooner. The Ministry of Justice says the change avoids the time needed to set up a new judge-only division of the crown court.

segments.title: Backlog and remaining reforms
segments.body: There are nearly 81,000 cases in the crown courts, a figure projected to reach 100,000 without reform. Judge-only trials will remain possible in a small number of lengthy, technical fraud cases. The government will still remove defendants’ right to choose a crown court jury trial for some “either way” offences, and plans to increase magistrates’ sentencing powers.

The Bar Council welcomed the change on jury trials but called increased magistrates’ sentencing powers and removal of defendants’ choice a dangerous experiment, warning of risks to trust and existing disparities. Victims’ commissioner Claire Waxman questioned whether the remaining plan would be sufficient to deliver swifter justice.

content.headline: Tories signal deeper government cuts as Badenoch prepares conference pitch
content.shortHeadline: Tories signal cuts beyond £47bn pledge
content.standfirst: Leaked comments by shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith point to savings beyond the £47bn already announced. The Conservatives say they want a smaller state, while polling suggests Kemi Badenoch has improved her standing but the party remains behind Labour and Reform.

image.caption: Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith’s leaked comments point to further Conservative spending cuts.

sources.originalTitle: Tories plan to extend cuts beyond £47bn previously pledged, leak reveals
Badenoch returns to Conservative conference much stronger than a year ago

segments.body: The Conservatives are seeking cuts beyond the £47bn already announced, according to leaked remarks by shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith. He told party members that ministers had discussed finding further savings “in every part of government”. A party spokesperson confirmed the Tories wanted additional savings, including from welfare and what they call wasteful spending.

segments.title: A conference test for Badenoch
segments.body: The Conservatives have proposed reducing welfare spending, cutting civil service jobs and international aid, and scrapping most of Labour’s clean-energy programme. The Guardian reports that Badenoch’s personal ratings have improved and the party has risen from the mid-teens to the low 20s in some polls, but the party brand remains a problem and Reform continues to compete for right-leaning voters.

perspectives.body: Polling and focus-group analysis cited by The Guardian suggests Badenoch has become better known and more positively regarded by some potential Conservative voters. The report also notes that insiders see her leadership as vulnerable if the party cannot sustain gains against Reform.

content.headline: Badenoch proposes £700m childcare expansion for higher earners
content.shortHeadline: Tories would extend free childcare to higher earners
content.standfirst: The Conservative plan would remove England’s £100,000 earnings cut-off for free childcare, allowing eligible working parents to claim regardless of income. The party says it would fund the £700m annual cost by cutting jobs at public bodies.

image.caption: Kemi Badenoch meets parents and toddlers ahead of the Conservative conference.

sources.originalTitle: Tories would expand free childcare to high earners, Badenoch says

segments.body: The Conservatives say they would abolish the £100,000 earnings limit for free childcare in England. Under the proposal, parents working at least 16 hours a week could claim the entitlement even if one parent earns above the current threshold. Kemi Badenoch says the existing cut-off can deter parents from taking a pay rise or promotion.

The party estimates the change would cost £700m a year and says it would be funded by cutting jobs at organisations including Arts Council England and the Environment Agency. Labour criticised the proposal as a priority for higher earners. The proposal follows the Conservatives’ earlier plan to abolish most stamp duty on primary homes in England and Northern Ireland.

content.headline: Tories split over whether to keep pension triple lock as Burnham proposes reform
content.shortHeadline: Tories divided over future of pension triple lock
content.standfirst: Kemi Badenoch has reaffirmed the Conservatives’ commitment to the triple lock, despite senior figures arguing it may be unaffordable. Andy Burnham’s proposed change from 2030 has reopened a debate about pension rises, public spending and the cost of a national care service.

image.caption: Senior Conservatives are debating whether to maintain the pension triple lock.

sources.originalTitle: Badenoch wants to save the triple lock. But senior Tories want it gone

segments.body: Senior Conservatives have urged Kemi Badenoch to keep options open on the state pension triple lock, but the party has reaffirmed its commitment to the policy. The current system raises pensions by whichever is highest: average wage growth, inflation or 2.5%. Andy Burnham has proposed using inflation or 2.5% from 2030, removing the wages link.

Some Conservative figures say the triple lock is unaffordable over the long term, while others worry a change would alienate older voters, who were among the party’s strongest groups at the 2024 election. The policy debate also centres on whether pension savings could meaningfully pay for Burnham’s proposed national care service; the article cites estimates suggesting a substantial gap.

content.headline: UK households face further energy bill pressure as winter costs loom
content.shortHeadline: Energy suppliers warn UK bills could rise further
content.standfirst: Energy UK says annual bills could reach £2,100 by January, while forecasts point to a 16% rise next year. The group wants targeted rebates and debt relief; ministers say recent measures have already reduced costs.

image.caption: Energy suppliers are calling for more help with household bills.

sources.originalTitle: The three measures Burnham could use to cut energy bills
Truckers plea for fuel duty bailout as diesel prices hit record high

segments.body: Energy UK has urged the government to offer more help to households as suppliers warn that typical annual bills could rise to £2,100 by January. The current average is £1,723 after a recent increase; forecasts cited by The i Paper predict a further 16% rise, or £276, next year. The supplier group says customer debt could reach £7bn by year-end.

segments.title: Calls for targeted help
segments.body: Energy UK wants targeted rebates beyond the Warm Home Discount and a debt-relief scheme for the most affected households. It has previously called for £450 a year in rebates for households in need. The government says its VAT cut will reduce the annual price cap by £45 and points to £150 of costs removed from bills earlier this year.

The reports link higher energy costs to disrupted supplies during the US-led war with Iran. Energy UK warns that storage will take time to replenish and bills could remain high into spring. The government says it is considering further steps while pursuing longer-term reductions through clean power.

content.headline: Avanti nationalisation will not quickly fix delays or cut fares, experts warn
content.shortHeadline: Avanti nationalisation is no quick fix for rail passengers
content.standfirst: The operator has the UK’s worst on-time record, but experts say infrastructure constraints on the West Coast Main Line are a major cause of delays. Public ownership may improve coordination, but fare reductions and service improvements are not guaranteed.

image.caption: Avanti West Coast had the worst on-time performance among operators last year.

sources.originalTitle: The UK’s worst rail firm is being nationalised. But don’t expect improvements soon

segments.body: Avanti West Coast is due to return to public ownership in March after a poor performance record. Only 37.9% of its trains were on time in 2025–26, the worst result of any operator, and 5.6% were cancelled. The government says a state-run service will work better for passengers, but rail experts caution that nationalisation alone will not fix the main causes of disruption.

segments.title: Infrastructure is the constraint
segments.body: Network Rail problems accounted for 66% of Avanti’s delayed minutes, according to the regulator. Experts point to congestion, signalling failures and limited capacity on the West Coast Main Line. A £400m programme of renewals and upgrades is due to finish by March 2029, but one rail analyst says the work is mainly maintenance rather than a major expansion in capacity.

Bringing track and train under Great British Railways could improve coordination and help services recover from incidents, the experts say. But they do not expect public ownership to lower fares; they say that would require more public funding. The northern leg of HS2, which experts said could have eased pressure on the route, was scrapped by the previous Conservative government.

content.headline: Pharmacy closures leave some patients facing long journeys for medicines
content.shortHeadline: Pharmacy closures force patients to travel farther
content.standfirst: Fifty-one pharmacies in England closed between January and August, including 31 in areas supported by a scheme intended to protect access. In some communities, patients now face lengthy journeys for prescriptions and advice.

image.caption: More than 50 pharmacies in England have closed so far this year.

sources.originalTitle: The worst places to live if you are ill – where trips to chemists take an hour

segments.body: Analysis of NHS figures by the National Pharmacy Association found that 51 high-street pharmacies in England closed between January and August, about two a week. Thirty-one were in areas covered by the Pharmacy Access Scheme, which provides extra funding where there is no nearby alternative. The association says nearly 10 million people have lost a local pharmacy since 2016.

segments.title: Access and funding pressures
segments.body: A closure in Long Rock, Cornwall, has left patients facing a 17-mile round trip and up to 80 minutes on public transport to reach another pharmacy, according to the report. Community Pharmacy England says closures can make it harder to collect medicines and advice, and intensify health inequalities. It says pharmacies still face a funding gap despite a recent government increase.

content.headline: UK and EU discuss transition periods in food and drink trade talks
content.shortHeadline: UK and EU discuss transition periods for food trade
content.standfirst: The EU has dropped its opposition to transition periods as both sides negotiate closer alignment on animal, plant and health rules. The aim is to avoid a costly abrupt change for British businesses, though negotiations on youth mobility remain difficult.

image.caption: The UK and EU are negotiating agreements on food trade, youth mobility and carbon markets.

sources.originalTitle: Brexit deal inches closer as EU gives ground to UK on food and drink

segments.body: The UK and EU are negotiating an agreement to align British rules on animal, plant and health standards with EU law, with the aim of easing food and drink trade. EU opposition to transition periods has now been dropped, according to two sources quoted by The i Paper, allowing businesses time to adapt rather than face an abrupt switch.

Industry representatives have warned that immediate alignment could cost businesses between £500m and £810m a year. Transition periods are being discussed for areas including pesticides and long-shelf-life products. The two sides are aiming to agree packages on food trade, youth mobility and carbon markets, but remain apart on student tuition fees and visa numbers.

content.headline: High electricity prices spur renewed interest in rooftop solar in Denmark
content.shortHeadline: High power prices boost demand for rooftop solar
content.standfirst: Solar installers say more households are moving from enquiries to installations as electricity prices rise. Cheaper batteries are improving the economics, while locally used rooftop power could also ease pressure on the electricity grid.

image.caption: Solplus director Kasper Bruhn says interest in home solar panels is rising.

sources.originalTitle: Solceller er populære: Vi gør det for pengepungens skyld

segments.body: Danish solar companies report a rise in household interest as electricity prices reach their highest peak-period levels in two years. Solplus director Kasper Bruhn says more customers are proceeding with installations, not just asking about them. The Danish Solar Association also says consumers are again looking for ways to reduce their electricity costs.

Falling battery prices have helped make solar panels more attractive to households by allowing them to store midday electricity for use during morning and evening peaks. One new customer told DR that saving money was the main reason for installing panels, although he also welcomed the contribution to the green transition.

A lecturer at DTU Elektro says electricity used in the building where it is generated does not need to be transported through a grid that is already constrained. He estimates that suitable private rooftops could produce around 10–15% of the electricity expected to be used in Denmark in 2030.

content.headline: Denmark urges 800,000 commuters to claim higher travel tax deduction
content.shortHeadline: 800,000 Danish commuters urged to update tax estimates
content.standfirst: Commuters who update their preliminary tax assessments can receive a temporarily increased travel deduction through their monthly pay. The government says the measure is aimed at people most affected by rising fuel costs.

sources.originalTitle: 800.000 pendlere har penge til gode, og skatteministeren vil 'meget gerne af med dem'

segments.body: About 800,000 Danish commuters have not updated their preliminary tax assessments to receive a temporarily higher commuting deduction, Tax Minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt says. Around 200,000 people have already made the change. A typical commuter could be entitled to between 2,500 and 3,000 kroner, according to the minister.

The higher deduction applies in 2026 and was adopted by the government to help commuters facing higher petrol and diesel prices. Those who update their assessment can see the effect in their pay; others will receive the money through their tax return next year. The minister defended targeting people who travel farther rather than cutting fuel tax for everyone.

content.headline: Danish psychologist challenges plan to spend one billion kroner on child mental-
content.shortHeadline: Psychologist says child mental health plan should do more
content.standfirst: A family therapist argues that children’s distress cannot be addressed by psychiatric services alone and calls for greater support for parents, schools and local services. The health minister says the emergency plan includes both treatment and community-based help.

image.caption: Family therapist Allan Holmgren argues for broader support for parents and children.

sources.originalTitle: Psykolog: Hjælp forældrene i stedet for at bruge én milliard på psykiatrien

segments.body: Psychologist Allan Holmgren says a one-billion-kroner emergency plan for child and adolescent mental health risks treating distress too narrowly as a psychiatric problem. He argues that children’s wellbeing is also shaped by family life, schools and childcare settings, and that prevention and support for parents should receive greater attention.

segments.title: Government defends the plan
segments.body: Health Minister Ida Auken says the plan is intended both to reduce long waits for psychiatric assessment and to provide accessible community services with a family focus. Holmgren acknowledges that some children need diagnosis and psychiatric treatment, but says the response should also address the conditions of their everyday lives.

content.headline: Danish couple buys coastal plot despite long-term flood projections
content.shortHeadline: Danish couple buys coastal plot despite flood risk
content.standfirst: The buyers plan to build a raised summer house despite projections of higher sea levels and flood risk near Kerteminde. A housing economist says prices in exposed areas should reflect future climate costs, but the research is not yet complete.

sources.originalTitle: Har købt sommerhusgrund i første række – i fremtiden risikerer den ikke længere at findes

segments.body: Niels Bækholm and his wife bought a plot on Langø, near Kerteminde, close to the water, and plan to build a summer house on a raised foundation. Bækholm says he understands there is a risk but bought the property for family enjoyment, not as an investment. The article cites a study warning that Kerteminde could lose homes to flooding by 2100.

segments.title: How climate risk affects value
segments.body: A local estate agent says demand for waterfront holiday homes remains strong, and the plot and the couple’s former summer house both sold above asking price. Housing Economics Knowledge Centre director Curt Liliegreen argues that prices in climate-exposed areas should fall over time so future losses are smaller. He says early analysis points to a price effect, but it may not be dramatic and the research is unfinished.

content.headline: Experts warn illegal IPTV services could expose Danish users to cyber risks
content.shortHeadline: Illegal IPTV may expose Danish users to cyber risks
content.standfirst: A report commissioned by a content-protection group warns that illegal streaming services can expose users’ data and potentially be used to carry cyberattacks or manipulate content. Researchers say no concrete example of manipulated TV signals has yet been identified.

image.caption: Illegal IPTV services offer access to large numbers of television channels.

sources.originalTitle: Tusindvis bruger tjenesten – nu advarer eksperter om overhængende risiko

segments.body: Nearly 300,000 Danish households are estimated to pay for illegal IPTV, according to figures cited by TV 2. A report commissioned by Nordic Content Protection warns that providers may collect user data or use customers’ internet connections for cyberattacks. The report’s authors also say the services could be used to alter content before it reaches viewers.

segments.title: Warnings and questions about incentives
segments.body: The report’s researchers say artificial-intelligence tools could make real-time manipulation of streamed content more feasible, but TV 2 says no concrete example of manipulated signals on illegal services has been found. A technology commentator argues that the industry’s fragmented and increasingly expensive subscriptions push some consumers towards piracy; Nordic Content Protection rejects that as a justification for using criminal services.

perspectives.body: The report was commissioned by Nordic Content Protection, an organisation that works against illegal distribution. The article includes a media analyst’s criticism that the legal industry’s prices and fragmented sports packages contribute to piracy, and records the organisation’s disagreement.

content.headline: Women in Aarhus area change running routines after reported assaults
content.shortHeadline: Reported assaults unsettle women running in Aarhus
content.standfirst: Women in Trøjborg say they are avoiding evening runs or changing routes after two reported incidents near Riis Skov. Police are investigating the cases together but have not confirmed whether they are connected.

sources.originalTitle: Kvinder frygter løbetur efter flere episoder: - Det er virkelig uhyggeligt

segments.body: Women in the Aarhus neighbourhood of Trøjborg say they feel unsafe running after two reported assaults near Riis Skov. One incident in July involved a 22-year-old woman who police say was knocked down, restrained and groped; a similar incident involving a 24-year-old runner was reported on 27 September.

Some local women say they are choosing daylight hours or changing their routes. East Jutland Police are investigating the cases together and plan to increase patrols in the area. Police have not confirmed whether the incidents are connected and ask people to report suspicious activity.

content.headline: University study challenges official estimate of Danish border-shopping tax
content.shortHeadline: Study finds border shopping costs Denmark less tax revenue
content.standfirst: Researchers estimate that border shopping on sweets, soft drinks and beer cost the Danish state far less in 2019 than the tax ministry calculated. The study uses pandemic-era shopping patterns, when cross-border purchases were unavailable.

image.caption: Researchers and tax authorities differ over the effect of cross-border shopping on tax revenue.

sources.originalTitle: Studie af danskeres indkøbsvaner tegner nyt billede af grænsehandel

segments.body: A University of Copenhagen study estimates that Denmark lost 415 million kroner in 2019 tax revenue to cross-border shopping on goods including sweets, soft drinks and beer, compared with the Tax Ministry’s estimate of 1.16 billion kroner. The researchers say their measure examines how much spending moved to Danish shops when border shopping was not possible.

The study found the effect was concentrated among households living within 30 kilometres of the German border; it measured no change for households 120 kilometres or more away. The researchers say border shopping should therefore play a smaller role in decisions about taxes on these goods, while stressing that their findings do not prescribe a particular tax rate.

content.headline: Three teenagers charged over alleged shootings at family home in Kastrup
content.shortHeadline: Three teenagers charged over Kastrup family shooting
content.standfirst: Prosecutors allege three teenagers took part in an attempted killing for hire after 15 shots were fired into a home where a couple and their three children were sleeping. All three deny guilt; no motive is stated in the indictment.

image.caption: The Kastrup apartment building was hit by gunfire in March.

sources.originalTitle: Teenagere forsøgte at slå familie med tre børn ihjel i Kastrup, lyder anklage

segments.body: Three young men have been charged with attempted murder over a shooting at a family home in Kastrup on 31 March. Prosecutors allege that 15 rounds from an AK-47 went through the windows of the apartment while a couple and their three children were inside. No one was hit. The indictment says the attack was commissioned for payment, but gives no reason for the targeting.

segments.title: Other alleged attacks and court proceedings
segments.body: Two of the defendants are also accused of involvement in other attempted killings in the Copenhagen area and a fire in Roskilde in the days before the Kastrup shooting. The indictment describes each defendant’s alleged role; all three deny the charges. Copenhagen City Court is scheduled to begin the trial on 25 January.

content.headline: Venom’s Cronos made metal dangerous again — and helped invent black metal
content.shortHeadline: How Venom’s Cronos made metal dangerous again
content.standfirst: Conrad “Cronos” Lant, who has died aged 63, gave Venom its confrontational sound and theatrical menace. His influence reached far beyond the band, though he rejected the violence later associated with some of its admirers.

image.caption: Venom frontman Cronos pictured in 1985.

sources.originalTitle: No one could terrify like Cronos, the black metal innovator who reignited rock’s hellraising attitude
Conrad ‘Cronos’ Lant, frontman of UK heavy metal band Venom, dies aged 63

segments.body: When Venom erupted from Newcastle in the late 1970s, singer and bassist Conrad “Cronos” Lant thought heavy metal had gone soft. The band fused punk’s unruly DIY spirit with crude, hammering riffs and occult lyrics, making their music raw and deliberately alarming.

segments.title: An influence beyond the band
segments.body: Venom’s 1982 album Black Metal gave a name to a subgenre, while the band’s speed and ferocity helped inspire thrash acts including Metallica, Slayer and Anthrax. Cronos did not endorse the violence of some later Norwegian black metal musicians; he lamented that they were known for it rather than for their music.

content.headline: Erasure’s Andy Bell and Vince Clarke on grief, friendship and a new album
content.shortHeadline: Erasure’s 40-year friendship, through grief and change
content.standfirst: As Erasure return with their 20th album, Andy Bell and Vince Clarke reflect on the bond that carried them through bereavement. Clarke will direct the coming tour remotely after deciding not to travel.

image.caption: Erasure’s Vince Clarke and Andy Bell.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s a deep soul connection’: Erasure on how 40 years of friendship got them through grief – and why Vince Clarke has quit touring

segments.body: Erasure’s four decades together have been built around a striking contrast: Vince Clarke’s precision-tooled synth pop and Andy Bell’s flamboyant, emotionally open performances. Their friendship became especially important after Clarke’s wife, Tracy Hurley Martin, died of cancer in 2024; Bell, who lost his partner in 2012, supported him through grief.

segments.title: A different kind of tour
segments.body: The duo’s new album, Radio!! Radio!!, is their 20th. Clarke will not attend the accompanying UK and European arena tour, instead serving as musical director remotely while keyboard technician Howard Rider plays on stage. Bell says it will not feel the same without his longtime collaborator.

content.headline: Liz Harris on Grouper, streaming fraud and the restorative joy of Helen
content.shortHeadline: Liz Harris on streaming scams and the joy of making music together
content.standfirst: A viral Grouper track brought new listeners — and a scammer who tried to claim its royalties. Reuniting with her dream-pop trio Helen has offered Liz Harris a different lesson: collaboration can be restorative.

image.caption: Liz Harris of Helen and Grouper.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s rational to fear the music industry’: Grouper’s Liz Harris on virality, streaming scammers and her ‘restorative’ dream-pop trio

segments.body: Liz Harris has kept Grouper’s hushed, solitary music at a distance from the industry. When her 2008 song “Poison Tree” took off on TikTok, she learned that someone else had fraudulently uploaded and registered it, earning around six figures. Harris and her label were able to shut down the scam and recover what she was owed.

segments.title: The relief of making music together
segments.body: Harris’s other current project, Helen, is a dream-pop trio whose new album, Linda’s Head, grew out of the pleasure of working with friends. The rehearsals helped lift her spirits while she was dealing with medical difficulties. She describes the collaboration as restorative, and a welcome counterweight to Grouper’s intensely solitary sound.

content.headline: Soft Cell’s final album became a farewell to Dave Ball and 1980s New York
content.shortHeadline: Soft Cell’s last album is Marc Almond’s farewell to Dave Ball
content.standfirst: Marc Almond and Dave Ball had finished Danceteria together just two days before Ball died. Almond says he would not make another Soft Cell album without his bandmate; this one revisits the New York scene that shaped them.

image.caption: Soft Cell’s Marc Almond and Dave Ball.

sources.originalTitle: Soft Cell’s Marc Almond: ‘We finished the album – two days later Dave passed away’

segments.body: Soft Cell had agreed their new record was finished when keyboardist Dave Ball died in October 2025, two days later. Singer Marc Almond calls Danceteria the duo’s sixth and final album: he says he would not make another Soft Cell record without Ball. Its songs look back to the pair’s adventures in early-1980s New York.

segments.title: A city that changed the band
segments.body: Almond describes New York’s clubs as a revelation after the comparatively constrained London scene. The city’s exuberance and darkness fed the record, alongside the fear and loss as the AIDS crisis took hold. He says the pair were closer while making Danceteria than they had been for some time, and feels relieved they completed it together.

content.headline: Lulu’s comeback album gives her the creative control she long wanted
content.shortHeadline: Lulu returns with a record on her own terms
content.standfirst: After decades of being steered towards material she did not choose, the singer is setting the direction of a new album with her songwriter brother. She also reflects on addiction, recovery and the relief of speaking openly.

image.caption: Lulu, who began her career as a teenager in London.

sources.originalTitle: Lulu: ‘I’m not proud of being an alcoholic – but I’m not ashamed’

segments.body: At 77, Lulu is enjoying an unexpected return to the charts: “I’m in Love Again”, her first single in 10 years, has been popular on BBC Radio 2. It is the first taste of Let the Girl Sing Out, a January album she is co-writing with her brother Billy Lawrie and shaping herself.

segments.title: Facing the past
segments.body: Lulu says writing her memoir brought difficult experiences into the open, including the domestic abuse she witnessed as a child and the alcohol addiction she hid for decades before getting sober in 2013. She says she is not proud of being an alcoholic, but is no longer ashamed. Music, she says, has repeatedly given her a new beginning.

content.headline: Elvis Costello’s 49th-anniversary box set traces the making of My Aim Is True
content.shortHeadline: Elvis Costello’s debut, heard as a work in progress
content.standfirst: A 104-track edition of My Aim Is True adds demos, live recordings and early band material to the familiar debut. The review finds a revealing portrait of a young songwriter gradually assembling his sound and persona.

sources.originalTitle: My Aim Is True (49th Anniversary Edition)

segments.body: The new five-CD set puts Elvis Costello’s 1977 debut in the context of the songs and experiments that preceded it. Early recordings with Flip City show a craftsman working through country-tinged folk and American songwriter influences before punk and new wave sharpened his style.

segments.title: A transformation in progress
segments.body: The review sees the collection’s best material in its demos and outtakes, which make Costello’s rise feel gradual rather than miraculous. Later discs tracing his developing persona and work with backing band Clover add context, though the live reunion recording is more of a fan’s extra than an essential part of the story.

content.headline: The Beatles’ Rubber Soul still shifts shape in an expansive new reissue
content.shortHeadline: Rubber Soul’s many versions make a case for its restless greatness
content.standfirst: A deluxe edition gathers UK and US tracklists, stereo and mono mixes, outtakes and a new remix. The review argues that the album’s contradictions — and the choices behind it — are part of its enduring appeal.

sources.originalTitle: Rubber Soul (Super Deluxe)

segments.body: Rubber Soul was made under pressure: the Beatles completed the recordings and mixes within days, with a Christmas release deadline looming. Yet small choices in performance and arrangement helped the album become a turning point for the band and for what pop could encompass.

segments.title: No single definitive version
segments.body: The set includes the UK and US albums, their mono and stereo mixes, outtakes and a new remix. The US edition’s changed tracklist makes it feel like a different record, while alternate takes reveal the band working through ideas. The review’s conclusion: there is no one “real” Rubber Soul — listeners have their own.

content.headline: Lambchop strip back their sound, but Kurt Wagner’s stories stay expansive
content.shortHeadline: Lambchop go acoustic without shrinking Kurt Wagner’s world
content.standfirst: Punching the Clown pares the band’s arrangements back to acoustic guitar, banjo and choir. The review finds that the spare setting sharpens Wagner’s strange, funny and often moving storytelling.

sources.originalTitle: Punching the Clown

segments.body: Lambchop have moved among alt-country, slowcore, lounge and electronic experimentation over a 40-year career. On Punching the Clown, Kurt Wagner’s voice is unobscured by effects, set against Andrew Broder’s acoustic guitar, Justin Vernon’s banjo and choral harmonies.

segments.title: Humour beside grief
segments.body: Wagner’s songs keep their winding, unpredictable quality in the quieter setting. “The New World Wave” moves between family history, loss and absurd asides; elsewhere, images of illness and decay sit beside jokes and sudden tenderness. The review calls this the band’s most emotionally direct album, even as it remains among their most mysterious.

content.headline: Brassed Off at 30: Mark Herman on a film about more than a brass band
content.shortHeadline: Brassed Off still speaks to towns left behind
content.standfirst: The writer-director says the 1996 film’s appeal lies in its universal story of people being downtrodden. As it returns to the Royal Albert Hall with live music, he worries that mid-budget British films like it would struggle to get made now.

image.caption: Pete Postlethwaite in Brassed Off.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I thought Brassed Off might be popular within a 10 mile radius of Barnsley’: the director of Andy Burnham’s favourite film on its 30-year anniversary

segments.body: Mark Herman expected Brassed Off to find a modest audience near Barnsley. Instead, the 1996 story of a colliery brass band became a lasting British hit, blending comedy with the consequences of pit closures and the collapse of a community’s livelihood.

segments.title: A return to the Albert Hall
segments.body: For the anniversary, Grimethorpe Colliery Band — the group that inspired the film — will perform its music at the Royal Albert Hall alongside a screening. Herman says the story continues to connect with younger viewers, but fears there is little room in the British industry today for the mid-budget films he wants to make.

content.headline: Behemoth! review: Pedro Pascal’s classical-music drama misses its mark
content.shortHeadline: Behemoth! has a star and a score, but no clear direction
content.standfirst: Tony Gilroy’s return to feature directing pairs a cello maestro with grief, desire and family drama. The review finds its fractured structure and shifting tone leave the film feeling aimless.

image.caption: Pedro Pascal in Behemoth!.

sources.originalTitle: Behemoth! review - Pedro Pascal classical music drama hits all the wrong notes

segments.body: Pedro Pascal plays Alex, a cello player back in Los Angeles after years on the road. His work scoring screen productions brings him close to his family, while memories of a former lover and questions about her daughter complicate his return.

segments.title: A structure that won’t settle
segments.body: The review argues that abrupt timeline shifts and tonal lurches prevent the story from building emotional force. A promising cast and a score by a group of composers cannot compensate for subplots that feel underdeveloped or a central character who remains a distant spectator to his own life.

content.headline: Paul Thomas Anderson’s Cameron Winter concert film captures a rare stillness
content.shortHeadline: Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall makes a concert feel timeless
content.standfirst: Shot on 35mm, the 75-minute film preserves the Geese frontman’s solo performance with little added commentary or spectacle. The review finds its attentive quiet and striking images make it an unusually affecting concert document.

image.caption: A still from Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall.

sources.originalTitle: Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall review – Paul Thomas Anderson’s sumptuous recording is an immediate classic

segments.body: Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall records the Geese frontman’s solo acoustic concert, filmed by Paul Thomas Anderson and a small team. The film largely leaves the performance alone, relying on close shots, shifting light and Winter’s voice and piano rather than interviews or narration.

segments.title: A document for the devoted
segments.body: The review says the film preserves the audience’s concentrated silence as well as the music’s contrasts, turning a concert into something like a shared ritual. Its lack of context may leave newcomers without an entry point, but fans of Winter’s singular voice get an exquisitely rendered record of the performance.

content.headline: Bassam Tariq turns a stalled Blade project into an intimate thriller
content.shortHeadline: How Bassam Tariq reshaped Blade plans into a personal film
content.standfirst: Mahershala Ali plays a devout Muslim father who works as a contract killer in Tariq’s new Houston-set thriller. The director says the abandoned Marvel project helped shape its action — and that the smaller film proved a better fit.

image.caption: Bassam Tariq at the Toronto film festival in September 2026.

sources.originalTitle: How Bassam Tariq pivoted from stalled Blade reboot to new Mahershala Ali thriller: ‘I’m happier I made this movie’

segments.body: Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother follows Latif, a widowed father who sees his violence as divine retribution. Director Bassam Tariq says the story grew from his own frantic search for breast milk when his infant son was unwell, and from the need to be present as a father.

segments.title: What survived from Blade
segments.body: Tariq and Ali had worked together on Marvel’s long-delayed Blade reboot, which Tariq left in 2022. He says the fight choreography and preparation for that project carried over into their new film. He is happier with the result, describing the smaller production as a place where he could explore faith, grief and fatherhood with greater freedom.

content.headline: Digger divides critics over Tom Cruise’s oil-tycoon eco-satire
content.shortHeadline: Digger: a daring Cruise performance or an overblown misfire?
content.standfirst: Alejandro G Iñárritu’s climate satire gives Cruise a paunchy oil baron and a world-threatening crisis. One review calls it laborious and shallow; another embraces its eccentric scale and blunt political force.

image.caption: Tom Cruise as oil tycoon Digger Rockwell.

sources.originalTitle: Digger review – Tom Cruise’s loudmouth oil tycoon goes hard in Alejandro G Iñárritu’s eco-satire
Digger review: Tom Cruise takes the 'biggest risk of his career' in this 'love-it-or-hate-it' folly ★★★★☆

segments.body: Tom Cruise plays Digger Rockwell, an oil tycoon whose company has helped trigger a climate catastrophe. The film follows the mogul as he joins the response to a vast iceberg threatening northern Europe. The BBC review sees an eccentric, politically blunt satire whose wild performance and elaborate twists take it far from Cruise’s recent action roles.

perspectives.body: The Guardian review finds the satire shallow and laborious, arguing that a late narrative turn weakens the drama and leaves some of the film’s claims about oil and renewables insufficiently challenged.

segments.title: Two sharply different verdicts
segments.body: Both reviews note the film’s outsized style and Cruise’s transformation into a balding, paunchy Texan. The Guardian sees glibness and self-congratulation where the BBC finds daring excess and a resonant scenario. The BBC reviewer enjoyed the film despite its length; the Guardian reviewer found its ambition undercut by the execution.

perspectives.body: The BBC review describes Digger as a love-it-or-hate-it folly and argues that its unusual scale and political bluntness make it worth embracing, even when some excesses run too long.

content.headline: Why horror films keep landing in the Golden Globes’ comedy category
content.shortHeadline: The Golden Globes leave horror with an absurd awards choice
content.standfirst: Obsession is being submitted as a musical or comedy despite its violent story of forced love and murder. The Globes’ categories, this argument says, leave horror films choosing between a poor fit and a tougher path to recognition.

image.caption: A still from the horror film Obsession.

sources.originalTitle: Horror films like Obsession are shut out of the Golden Globes – unless they pretend to be comedies

segments.body: The Golden Globes divide major film categories between drama and musical or comedy, leaving horror with no natural home. Obsession, a dark story of a man using a magical object to make a woman love him, is being entered in musical or comedy — despite its violent consequences and scant comic relief.

segments.title: A genre without a comfortable fit
segments.body: The article argues that horror is often treated as insufficiently prestigious for drama, while its violence and unease make the comedy category an awkward alternative. That can affect awards momentum, even if a film’s individual performance — as with Demi Moore in The Substance — finds recognition there.

content.headline: James Dean beyond the rebel image: the vulnerable actor behind the icon
content.shortHeadline: The James Dean worth remembering is more than a rebel
content.standfirst: A look back at Dean’s brief career finds a searching performer shaped by Elia Kazan’s direction and caught off guard by fame. His most affecting moments, this account argues, reveal a vulnerable young man rather than a polished symbol.

image.caption: James Dean on the set of Giant in 1955.

sources.originalTitle: The truth about James Dean

segments.body: James Dean starred in only three films before dying in a car crash at 24, but his image as a restless outsider outlived the career. The account revisits his work with Elia Kazan on East of Eden, where the director drew on Dean’s difficult relationship with his father to reach the character of Cal.

segments.title: The person behind the image
segments.body: Dean’s fame grew rapidly after East of Eden, and his death helped turn him into a mythic figure. The essay points instead to the rawness of his performances: in a scene where Cal’s father rejects a gift, Dean breaks down and reaches for him. That moment, it suggests, is more revealing than the familiar pose of the cool rebel.

content.headline: Sense and Sensibility review: a darker Austen with a modern pulse
content.shortHeadline: Sense and Sensibility still speaks to the social-media age
content.standfirst: Georgia Oakley’s new adaptation is darker and less assured than the celebrated 1995 film, but its story of two sisters balancing feeling and restraint still resonates. The review finds Austen’s dilemmas strikingly familiar to modern readers.

image.caption: Daisy Edgar-Jones as Elinor Dashwood in Sense and Sensibility.

sources.originalTitle: Every millennial should read Sense and Sensibility

segments.body: Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles play Elinor and Marianne Dashwood, sisters with opposing approaches to emotion and romance. After their family loses its fortune, each must navigate love and security in a society that leaves women with few options.

segments.title: Sense and sensibility now
segments.body: The review connects Austen’s sisters to a modern tension between keeping feelings private and sharing everything, while financial uncertainty makes stability hard to secure. The film is described as darker and sometimes uneven, but its account of Marianne misreading a charming suitor’s intentions remains painfully recognisable.

content.headline: Friday Night Lights at 20: the small-town football drama that broke the rules
content.shortHeadline: Friday Night Lights made small-town Texas feel real
content.standfirst: Peter Berg’s series turned a book about football and community pressure into an unusually naturalistic drama. Its improvisation, strong ensemble and unvarnished sense of place helped launch careers and outlast a troubled run.

image.caption: Kyle Chandler and Connie Britton in Friday Night Lights.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Brave from the beginning’: 20 years of Friday Night Lights – the sports drama that dared to be different

segments.body: First broadcast in 2006, Friday Night Lights made fictional Dillon, Texas, a place where high-school football shaped the town’s mood and young players carried the hopes of adults around them. The series drew on H G “Buzz” Bissinger’s reporting on Odessa, including its racism and the costs of putting football ahead of education.

segments.title: A naturalistic ensemble
segments.body: Director Peter Berg encouraged actors to adapt dialogue and reactions as long as the story’s beats remained intact. That looseness helped the performances feel fresh for a network drama. Kyle Chandler and Connie Britton anchor the show, while Jesse Plemons and Michael B Jordan were among the cast members whose careers grew through it.

content.headline: War review: a glossy divorce drama built for glorious overindulgence
content.shortHeadline: War turns a rich couple’s divorce into addictive TV
content.standfirst: Sienna Miller and Dominic West lead a drama of expensive lawyers, public feuds and ever-shifting legal tactics. The review calls it high-quality balderdash: a fast, entertaining escape that knows exactly how melodramatic it is.

image.caption: Sienna Miller, James McArdle and Phoebe Fox in War.

sources.originalTitle: War review – Sienna Miller and Dominic West’s hellish divorce drama is massive, massive fun

segments.body: War centres on a high-profile divorce between social-media mogul Morgan Henderson and film star Carla Duval. Their rival legal teams manoeuvre over money, reputation and the terms of a marriage, with the dispute spilling into a maze of personal and professional betrayals.

segments.title: Soap opera with money
segments.body: The review relishes the show’s intricate plotting, elaborate offices and gleefully unpleasant lawyers. It praises the performances from Miller, West and the supporting cast, and sees the series’ ripped-from-the-headlines flavour as an added source of fun rather than a demand for viewers to take sides.

content.headline: The Celebrity Traitors gets off to a chaotic start with Richard E Grant
content.shortHeadline: Richard E Grant’s Traitors blunder makes the show even better
content.standfirst: Grant accidentally tells Joe Lycett he is a Traitor almost immediately after his selection. The review argues that the mistake gives the celebrity edition a gripping early problem — and shows why the format still thrives on unpredictable behaviour.

image.caption: Richard E Grant in The Celebrity Traitors.

sources.originalTitle: Richard E Grant has already ruined The Celebrity Traitors. It’s brilliant

segments.body: Richard E Grant’s delight at joining The Celebrity Traitors was obvious from the start. After he and Maya Jama were chosen as Traitors, he told Joe Lycett the truth — a spectacular slip that left the other contestants trying to decide whether he was joking or had exposed himself.

segments.title: The game gets a new complication
segments.body: The review says Grant’s error gives the series an immediate storyline, while the other contestants supply early suspicion, comic banter and competing theories. A twist then asks the Traitors to recruit a third player, setting up a decision involving James Acaster and Amol Rajan.

content.headline: Nigella Lawson brings a welcome appetite to The Great British Bake Off
content.shortHeadline: Nigella’s Bake Off celebrates pleasure in food
content.standfirst: The new judge rejects the idea that a sweet treat needs to be labelled “naughty”. This argument sees Lawson’s unapologetic enjoyment as a refreshing counterpoint to a culture that increasingly tells women to restrict what they eat.

image.caption: Nigella Lawson brings her love of food to Bake Off.

sources.originalTitle: Nigella is dismantling skinny culture one ‘naughty cookie’ at a time

segments.body: Nigella Lawson’s arrival as a Bake Off judge has changed the show’s relationship with food, this review argues. On one episode she eats biscuits with visible enthusiasm and objects when Paul Hollywood describes cookies as “naughty”, saying people should take their pleasures where they can.

segments.title: A different message about pleasure
segments.body: The article contrasts Lawson’s appetite with the calorie-conscious language viewers often encounter around women and food. Her presence in the bright Bake Off tent, it argues, brings her celebration of indulgence into a mainstream setting — and makes the series feel like a small respite from pressure to be thinner.

content.headline: Youth: Sharon Horgan’s new comedy raises questions about who gets to look real
content.shortHeadline: Youth and the narrow idea of who gets to be an everywoman
content.standfirst: Horgan’s middle-aged literary agent faces family pressures and an unruly body, but the critic argues that her casting highlights television’s beauty standards. The piece credits the series’ ambition while questioning why relatable women must still look exceptional.

image.caption: Sharon Horgan in Youth.

sources.originalTitle: Sharon Horgan’s Youth has one big problem

segments.body: In Youth, Sharon Horgan plays Alex, a 50-something literary agent caught between her teenage son, ageing parents, work and a difficult love life. The i reviewer admires Horgan’s writing and performance, but argues that her striking appearance makes it harder to see Alex as the ordinary, frazzled everywoman the role suggests.

segments.title: Who gets to be ordinary?
segments.body: The criticism is aimed not at Horgan but at an industry that still expects women on screen to meet narrow beauty standards. The article notes Horgan’s own comments about the treatments she uses to look like a “human woman” on television, and argues that the medium needs room for women who look less polished and more like everyday viewers.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s future looks uncertain, but fans still believe it will return
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who is off air — and its future is unresolved
content.standfirst: The BBC has ended its Disney+ partnership, cancelled a planned Christmas special and is seeking outside production funding. Fans and former contributors differ on why the revival faltered, but the show’s next chapter remains an open question.

image.caption: Several actors who have played Doctor Who, including Ncuti Gatwa and Jodie Whittaker.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: Doctor Who has gone quiet since its 2025 series, with no confirmed new Doctor and no Christmas special planned. The BBC says it is seeking a partner to help fund future production after its collaboration with Disney+ ended, but no new company has yet stepped forward.

segments.title: What made the show endure?
segments.body: Fans and former contributors point to different explanations for the recent decline, including confusing scripts and the challenge of sustaining a long-running format. The article traces the show’s history of reinvention, from its 2005 return to changing Doctors and showrunners, and argues that its future depends on fresh stories as well as respect for its core identity.

content.headline: The Split Up brings a British Asian family to a new divorce-law drama
content.shortHeadline: The Split Up builds its own world around a British Asian family
content.standfirst: Ritu Arya and Sanjeev Bhaskar lead the Manchester-set spin-off, which keeps the original’s high-stakes family-law formula. Its creators say the new series aims to show British Asian characters living recognisable everyday lives, not just exceptional circumstances.

image.caption: Ritu Arya leads the cast of The Split Up.

sources.originalTitle: The Split is back – with a twist

segments.body: The Split Up centres on Aria Kishan, a barrister poised to take over her family’s Manchester law firm, until her mother’s death changes her father’s succession plans. The six-part spin-off mixes divorce cases with conflict among the Kishans, carrying forward the original show’s interest in ambition, love and betrayal.

segments.title: Representation beyond the usual roles
segments.body: Writer Ursula Rani Sarma says she wanted a British Asian family whose lives were not defined by terrorism or arranged marriage. The series has a predominantly British Asian cast and creative team, and Abi Morgan, who created The Split, says the spin-off’s central formula remains family, relationships and high-stakes cases.

content.headline: Carrie’s new screen life reopens the argument over who the heroine should be
content.shortHeadline: Carrie’s casting debate meets a new, modernised adaptation
content.standfirst: Mike Flanagan’s series has drawn criticism from readers who say Stephen King’s angry, physically “plain” heroine is repeatedly softened on screen. A horror scholar argues that the new version updates the story’s bullying for the social-media era.

image.caption: A still from the new Prime Video adaptation of Carrie.

sources.originalTitle: Why a new TV version of horror classic Carrie is already annoying people

segments.body: The new eight-part Carrie has prompted debate about its lead character’s appearance and temperament. King described Carrie White as a “chunky girl” and an angry teenager, while critics of earlier screen versions say the role has repeatedly gone to conventionally attractive actresses and made her seem more passive.

segments.title: Adaptation and its limits
segments.body: Mike Flanagan’s version changes Carrie’s backstory, including her being homeschooled before entering school after her father’s death, and brings social media into the story of her bullying. Horror scholar Sorcha Ní Fhlainn says the show can work on its own terms, while the article also notes market pressures and the loss of access to Carrie’s inner thoughts in screen adaptations.

content.headline: Gears of War: E-Day has its best combat yet, but repeats itself
content.shortHeadline: Gears of War: E-Day is thrilling to fight, tedious to explore
content.standfirst: The prequel delivers weighty guns, fluid movement and destructible environments, but its campaign repeatedly revisits the same streets. The review finds the series’ strongest combat surrounded by a safe and overlong experience.

image.caption: Marcus Fenix in Gears of War: E-Day.

sources.originalTitle: Gears of War: E-Day review – an alien invasion shouldn’t be this boring

segments.body: E-Day takes players to the alien invasion that has long haunted Gears of War lore. Its opening hours deliver the series’ familiar cover-based firefights with improved movement, detailed destruction and a satisfying sense of weight to the weapons.

segments.title: A campaign that runs out of ideas
segments.body: The review finds that the city setting becomes a constraint: routes and environments are revisited, exploration is cluttered with collectibles, and the game can punish players for wandering away from objectives. The combat remains excellent, but the campaign does too little to build on the ideas it introduces early.

content.headline: Ace Combat 8 turns the Top Gun fantasy into a surprisingly affecting game
content.shortHeadline: Ace Combat 8 soars with thrilling dogfights and a human story
content.standfirst: The aerial combat is fast, spectacular and accessible to newcomers, while a more cinematic story gives pilots and their relationships room to register. The review calls it a triumph, despite some confusion in battle and an untested online mode.

image.caption: A fighter jet in Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve.

sources.originalTitle: Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve review – brilliant aerial combat game fulfils the Top Gun fantasy

segments.body: Ace Combat 8 puts players in the role of a propaganda-invented ace pilot who becomes a real figure of hope in the fictional world of Strangereal. Its missions range from dogfights to bombing runs, with clear assistance for beginners and more demanding controls for series veterans.

segments.title: A story that lands
segments.body: The review praises the game’s cinematic presentation, expressive characters and soaring score, saying its story proves unexpectedly moving for an arcade flight-combat game. The battlefields can be visually confusing, and the reviewer could not test the online multiplayer mode, but the single-player experience is judged a triumph.

content.headline: Roblox scams are stealing children’s game currency and account details
content.shortHeadline: The fake Roblox links luring children into account theft
content.standfirst: Fraudsters promise free Robux through links on social platforms, then direct children to lookalike login pages. Security experts advise using the official app and treating authentication codes like passwords.

image.caption: Roblox advises users not to follow links from unknown senders or websites.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Mum, where did my Robux go?’ The Roblox scam targeting children

segments.body: The scam begins with an offer of free Robux, Roblox’s in-game currency, often posted in YouTube or TikTok comments or gaming chats. Children who follow the link may land on a convincing fake sign-in page; it redirects them to Roblox after collecting their login details.

segments.title: How to reduce the risk
segments.body: NordVPN researchers say they found almost 200 addresses selling ready-made phishing pages over seven days. Its experts advise opening Roblox directly through the official app or website and never sharing two-factor or backup codes. Roblox says it cannot guarantee recovery of lost currency or items.

content.headline: A father and son revisit the Call of Duty missions they first played together
content.shortHeadline: Replaying Call of Duty becomes a reunion for father and son
content.standfirst: Seventeen years after first tackling Modern Warfare 2 together, a father and his 22-year-old son return to the same co-op missions. The essay finds joy in the teamwork, the memories and the time they have left before living far apart.

image.caption: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, the game father and son played together.

sources.originalTitle: Playing video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tears

segments.body: The writer and his adult son return to Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, the first game they played together when the son was five. They retry co-op missions they never completed back then, discovering that a cautious scout and a fast-moving fighter can finally make a good team.

segments.title: A bond built through play
segments.body: The pair work out how to handle the game’s guard dogs, fail repeatedly and celebrate when they succeed. The writer says the sessions have brought back a carefree pleasure in gaming, and that his son expects to remember the time together as some of their best. They are due to move to different parts of the world in a few months.

content.headline: Meet the volunteer Pokémon professors who keep tournaments running
content.shortHeadline: The Pokémon tournament volunteers behind the battles
content.standfirst: At the world championships, volunteer professors teach players, judge disputes and help keep events safe. Their work requires game knowledge and patience — and the company did not provide details about how different groups are compensated.

image.caption: Players and visitors at the 2026 Pokémon world championships in San Francisco.

sources.originalTitle: Meet the real-life Pokémon professors, the unsung heroes of competitive monster-battling

segments.body: Around 300 Pokémon professors were present at the 2026 world championships in San Francisco, according to The Pokémon Company International. These volunteers help run tournaments as referees, teachers and event staff, with responsibilities ranging from technical support to checking results and maintaining a safe venue.

segments.title: Rules, support and difficult calls
segments.body: Head judge Gemma Byard says professors must make difficult rulings while helping players understand what happened. Evelyne de Groot compares the work to customer service, where clear instructions and knowledge of the game can shape competitors’ experience. The company declined to give an official account of how professors are compensated.

content.headline: Why players are rejecting games that tell them every move
content.shortHeadline: Players want games to leave room for discovery
content.standfirst: Viral clips of Marvel’s Wolverine mock its constant prompts and automated sequences. The argument here is that major games risk removing the agency, friction and satisfaction that make playing feel different from watching.

image.caption: Marvel’s Wolverine, criticised for its frequent prompts and guidance.

sources.originalTitle: Why fans are digging their claws into Wolverine over its patronising gameplay

segments.body: Marvel’s Wolverine became a target for clips showing objective markers, highlighted objects and a chase sequence that appears to continue without player input. The article says the ridicule reflects a wider frustration with blockbuster games that repeatedly tell players where to go and what to do.

segments.title: The value of friction
segments.body: The writer distinguishes difficulty from friction: challenge can come from demanding combat, while friction is the space a game leaves for players to find their way, learn and make decisions. Games such as Hollow Knight: Silksong and Blue Prince show how that space can be used differently. The hope is that the response to Wolverine reminds studios to trust players.

content.headline: Can a video-game romance count as cheating? GTA VI provokes debate
content.shortHeadline: GTA VI’s virtual romance exposes real relationship anxieties
content.standfirst: Social-media users argue that maintaining a relationship between the game’s protagonists crosses a line. The article calls the claim itself debatable, but says the reaction reflects broader concerns about loneliness and feeling neglected.

image.caption: Lucia and Jason, the couple at the centre of Grand Theft Auto VI.

sources.originalTitle: Grand Theft Auto VI: can playing a video game count as cheating on your partner?

segments.body: The prospect of romance between GTA VI protagonists Lucia and Jason has prompted claims on social media that playing the game could amount to “micro-cheating”. The planned interactions include dates, messages and gestures that strengthen the couple’s bond, and the article notes the game asks players to maintain the relationship whichever character they play.

segments.title: A debate about attention
segments.body: The writer considers in-game romance different from infidelity, while acknowledging that relationship boundaries vary. Sex educator Dee Whitnell argues that frustration may be understandable when a partner invests care in a fictional relationship that feels absent from real life. The article sees the controversy as a sign of wider loneliness and disconnection.

content.headline: Excavations reveal Lismore’s sixth-century monastery was a major centre
content.shortHeadline: Dig reveals Lismore monastery’s wider importance
content.standfirst: Community-led work on the Scottish island has uncovered early buildings, extensive burials and evidence of gold and silver craftworking. Archaeologists say the finds recast the monastery’s role in the spread of Christianity.

image.caption: Islanders and volunteers excavate the early medieval cemetery on Lismore.
